en: DA or LGU pages may advise moving animals out of flood plains before a typhoon, livelihood support that sits beside human evacuation orders.
Authorities also support communities by announcing when it is safer to return; gather that all-clear from the same official channels, not from a guess.
Other reliable sites include WMO summaries and academic hazard papers, but local support actions should still be confirmed on Philippine government pages.
Official pages frame evacuation as protection, a way authorities support people in mapped danger zones rather than as a punishment for staying.
The competency is about typhoon-affected communities, so a DOST scholarship page is the wrong source even though it is an official DOST website.
A strong class packet cites at least three official pages, such as PAGASA, NDRRMC, and DSWD, then says what support each one documents.
DOH or DSWD pages may mention psychosocial support in evacuation centers; if you include it, quote the named page and do not give medical advice yourself.
A poster can show screenshots of official homepages with the dates, plus one sentence each on warning, rescue, and relief as the three support layers.
Authorities support communities through recovery months with housing and livelihood programs, which later official reports still document after the headlines fade.
Better forecasts from DOST-PAGASA are themselves a form of support: earlier, clearer warnings give families more hours to move and to pack.
Some LGU pages list which office stays open as an emergency operations center, a practical support detail students can gather from the city site.
Before the season, NDRRMC and PAGASA sites post preparedness checklists, support that happens even when no named cyclone exists yet.
Quote one official sentence about support, then paraphrase in your own words, so the gathered fact stays tied to the agency and still reads as yours.
A complete answer names more than warnings: it also identifies relief, rescue, shelter, and recovery actions found on official websites.
Gathering here means opening DOST and other reliable sites, naming the authority, and recording how that office actually helps typhoon-hit communities.
Tidal energy needs a useful difference between high tide and low tide, the range secondary sources measure before anyone builds a plant.
A tidal barrage is built across a suitable estuary so the height difference drives turbines as the basin fills and empties.
Where a narrow channel speeds the tide, underwater turbines can harvest the current without a full barrage wall across a bay.
Secondary energy studies look for large tidal range or fast tidal streams, because a pretty beach with small tides cannot power a plant.
Tide times can be predicted years ahead from astronomy, so tidal energy is regular in a way wind energy is not, a point energy agencies often stress.
Many coasts have two highs and two lows each day, so a well-sited plant can generate on a repeating daily schedule of tidal difference.
A tidal lagoon uses a walled basin beside the coast so the same rise-and-fall difference turns turbines without closing an entire river mouth.
Secondary sources also warn that barrages can change mudflats and fish movement, so a good site must have both energy and an accepted environmental plan.
Even a strong tide is useless for electricity if there is no grid connection; energy studies list both the water resource and the nearby power lines.
South Korea's Sihwa tidal power plant is a documented barrage-style site that secondary sources use as a working example of exploiting tidal difference.
France's La Rance plant has generated electricity from tidal difference for decades, a classic secondary-source example of a barrage across an estuary.
Tidal-stream turbines need enough depth to stay submerged at low tide, a site filter that resource maps use besides current speed.
Busy shipping channels may have fast tides but are poor plant sites if turbines would block ships, a conflict energy papers routinely discuss.
Spring tides, when Sun and Moon align, make a larger tidal difference and thus more potential energy than neap tides in the same place.
Neap tides have a smaller high-to-low difference, so a plant's output is not the same every day even though the schedule stays predictable.
